utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. This morning we start some minutes later than usual because of technical problems here in the courtroom. And the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rave. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I greet everyone. I wish peace unto this house, and I wish that this trial and the judgement and the day end in keeping with God's will, not necessarily mine. I also welcome the witness and wish him a pleasant stay here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have three questions left over from yesterday before I move on to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, P996 is the exhibit I need displayed in e-court, page 3. This relates to the question I asked about the so-called Carter Agreement the witness said he was unable to answer at the moment. And we'll see if this is going to remind him of anything. What we see here is a diary. Can we see page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is Mr. Kingori's diary, where he mentioned, as a UN observer, this Carter Agreement. First of all, let me ask you, do you know Mr. Joseph Kingori, and was he a UN observer while you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From his diary we see that he refers to the control of movement towards Zepa in keeping with the so-called Carter Agreement; that's the four bullet point on the right side -- sorry, on the left side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday what the Carter Agreement means and we see from this diary that the Carter Agreement had to do with controlling movement towards Zepa. Can you now remember what the Carter Agreement is about?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I went to my diary and to my notebooks and I did not find any information about a meeting in which the Carter Agreement was mentioned, and I was not able yesterday to go, for example, on the internet to read the Carter Agreement. And from my memory now, I really don't know what is in the Carter Agreement. If there is information about movements towards Zepa, I really don't know. I was not able to find out yesterday. And I was not in a meeting -- at least I have no notes about being in a meeting in which the Carter Agreement was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you know nothing about that agreement, I will have no further questions about it. Just in response to Mr. McCloskey -- it's 6526 page of the transcript, lines 16 to 18, testimony of Mr. Kingori. Thank you. You said yesterday that the commander of the UNPROFOR decided that you should not control inside the area known as the Bandera Triangle, and then you added it was not the commander of the UNPROFOR but the commander of the DutchBat. Can you tell us, finally, who decided you should not patrol in the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I got my orders from the commander of the Dutch Battalion in the enclave and it might be possible that he got the orders from commander UNPROFOR, but I really don't know. I know that finally the commander of DutchBat ordered his troops not to patrol in the area. Although we tried it several times and I figured out yesterday some things in my notebook in which we tried to patrol inside the area, but it was commander of the Dutch Battalion I got the information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the commander of the DutchBat or perhaps the commander of the UN force who gave orders to the commander of the DutchBat have the right to change the mandate of the UNPROFOR force in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a change in the mandate. I think it was a way of acting inside the enclave. And, of course, I think that the DutchBat commander is free to do his job in the way he thinks is the best to do, and I don't think that they changed the mandate by not patrolling in an area. I think we tried several times do our job over there without making casualties on both sides, and we tried to negotiate with, inside, the army of the BiH, and outside with the VRS army, to do our job properly. And I think it's not correct if you state that he changed the mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, sorry for interrupting you. You were referring to page 6526, lines 16 to 18 on page 3 of today's transcript, but, in fact, this is not the right page because Mr. Kingori testified much earlier. Perhaps you should check at a later stage the right reference so that Mr. McCloskey and everybody can find the testimony of Mr. Kingori. But perhaps for now you should continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said yesterday you had the mandate to disarm the Muslims in the protected area in keeping with the agreement on demilitarisation. Will you just answer me to the best of your knowledge, was it your mandate or not?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was our mandate to disarm the Muslims in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that mandate consistent with the agreement on demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I don't know exactly what's in the agreement because I don't know the agreement 15 years later, and -- from my head, and I don't have it over here. So -- but I think, yes, it was in -- inconsistent with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If that was consistent with the agreement, did one of the parties, or perhaps the UNPROFOR commander who was in charge of demilitarisation in keeping with the agreement, did any one of them have the right to change that mandate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think everybody saw that in the transcript you see the last answer of the witness. "... but I think, yes, it was inconsistent with the agreement." But I'm quite sure that this was not what you intended to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was consistent with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now please answer the last question of Mr. Tolimir, if you recall it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the agreement was signed by the UN and not by commander UNPROFOR, so I don't think that commander UNPROFOR in Bosnia or the commander of the Dutch Battalion had a right to change the mandate, so I don't think they would change the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For your information, do you know this agreement was signed by General Morillon, the then force commander?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, I think this is what I mean. Maybe we are talking about different mandates, and I really don't know the mandate what we are talking now about. But the only thing I can say after 15 years, I don't have the mandate, I don't think that commanders on the ground are able to change mandates given or signed by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How do you then explain that the commander changed your mandate as far as this Bandera Triangle was concerned when it was not stipulated by the agreement and no one had the right to change the agreement without the consent of all parties?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, at the time I was a warrant officer 2nd Class, sergeant-major in the Dutch army, I had a lieutenant-colonel as a commander; and as you know, in the army it's not regular in a time that you do your job that all the time you get orders from your commander, you go into agreements or other things because you doubt about the orders commanders are giving you. I think when you have the opinion that the commander of the Dutch Battalion changed the mandate, I think you have to ask him the question, because I can't answer it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Serbs had given their approval to change the agreement so that you do not control the Muslims in the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions about this. There was one more question left over from yesterday. Mr. McCloskey asked for a reference concerning a witness who participated in the attack on Kravica which you described as never having participated in combat. It's 6213, lines 18 through 20 of the 16 October transcript. My question was: "Can you tell us in which places your battalion Biljeg was involved in combat?" The witness answered: "In Skelani and for a minor part in Kravica." The rest is not relevant to this subject. This is just for your information and for purposes of verification. We also discussed Mr. Naser Oric yesterday. I asked the witness if he was aware that Naser Oric had stated that he had not carried out demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask for 1D39 -- sorry, 329. 1D329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the document, I'd just like to correct the transcript. The reference is 5625, lines 17 and 18. That's Mr. Kingori's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While we are dealing with corrections, you see on page 6, line 16, a reference to hearing of the 16th of October. At that day, we had no hearing; but I think, Mr. Tolimir, you were referring to the 6th of October, if I'm not mistaken. Perhaps you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's right. I had in mind the 6th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Clearly the General has a list of documents he's going to be using for cross, so could we be provided that as per the court order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We provided Naser Oric's interview, 1D329. We provided it yesterday to Mr. McCloskey. We see it on the right-hand side here. And this is an interview given by Naser Oric to the daily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I interrupt you. The problem is that it is not part of your list of potential exhibits to be used with this witness. And I think Mr. McCloskey was asking for a complete list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Immediately before this witness appeared in the courtroom, that document was uploaded in e-court. If it cannot be used, I can certainly take Mr. McCloskey's request into consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no problem with this document or, really, any others, but I would like General Tolimir to follow the orders and the rules that we live by in this courtroom. We would like a list. We have no list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Didn't you receive any list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart didn't, and I don't see one immediately on my list. So if there is such a list, if they could send it to Ms. Stewart, I -- we'd be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber has received a list some days ago, but this specific document is not included in the list of the documents to be used with this witness. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just before the beginning of today's session, this document was uploaded in e-court. Since we were not confident that we would be able to do it early this morning, it's not on the list, and we didn't know whether we would be using it at all. Since the document was mentioned yesterday, Mr. Tolimir finally decided to show it to the witness today. An updated list will be provided to the OTP hopefully during this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, in cross-examination documents come up at the last minute and I don't -- wouldn't expect every document to be on a cross-examination list. I have no problem with that. I'm sure we'll be doing the same. But Ms. Stewart cannot find any list because she has none. So if we could just get whatever list you've got to her then we'll be fine and there should be no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this time there was just a mistake because the Chamber has received a list. Perhaps it was not sent to the OTP in time. But Mr. Gajic promised to do that during the first session of today. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said it -- thank you, Mr. President. As I've already said it, this is an interview entitled, "Naser Oric's confession." It was given to the daily "Oslobodenje" on Friday, 23rd of August, 1996. The ERN number is 0042-9641. I emphasise this because you can't see it in the right-hand-side corner. Can the document please be scrolled a little, the right-hand side to the left, and now you can see the ERN number. And can the document now please be scrolled up a little, we would like to see the entire content down to the signature. And I'm going to be using that particular passage in the text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The last passage has been blown up, and we will be reading from the text: "When UNPROFOR troops set up their check-points and observation posts, we immediately realised that we could not rely on them. A team of my lads who were not militarily trained but they were reliable ..." I can't read this, I'm sorry. "... reserve units decided to establish our lines, our own lines, to organise our own monitors. The system functioned in the following way: When an UNPROFOR patrol was approaching, our guys on the lines informed us so we could remove the weapons. If the UNPROFOR soldiers asked about the presence of our lads on those lines, we answered that we couldn't trust them and that we were afraid of Chetniks, so we wanted to have our own guards. They showed understanding for that, which was not the case when we dug our trenches and fortifications." My question for you, sir, is this: Did you know that Muslims were covering up all of their activities and that they were pretending to be just common folks, unarmed civilians? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that of course in the situation the former Yugoslavia was in both parties played the same game. In this statement in the newspaper, Naser Oric stated the way they acted. In a meeting from the 23rd of February, from the commander DutchBat with Naser Oric, he told that -- he told the population of the enclave that he trusts the UN, he will -- that the UN will defend the enclave so that they should hand over their weapons. And, of course, in the end we saw that they did not hands over all their weapons because there still were weapons, and the enclave was not demilitarised. But, of course, when they had weapons and when they did military activities, they would not show it to us and they would hide it, especially in the same way as also the Serbs did because we got the same information, only information, from commanders who tell us that nothing was going on and in the other way we discovered that they were frequently fighting and had fire fights.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are drawing a parallel here, were there any Serbs in the demilitarised zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated yesterday, when I saw the map, I saw two lines. We were not all talking about the same line of a demilitarised zone. The Serbs had their own ideas about it, the Muslims had their own ideas about it, and we were in between. We had our own map that we took over from our predecessors, and it was discussed several times with the Muslims and the Serbs. On the 28th of February, we had a meeting with Major Nikolic, and we had a discussion about the confrontation line, so also for them it was not exactly clear. Of course, they wanted more into the zone and the Muslims wanted them more out of the zone. The proposal was to look if we were talking about the same line, and we proposed that, especially in the western part, Major Sarkic from the Milici Brigade and an UNMO could go into the field to check if we were talking exactly about the same line and the same positions of the demilitarised zone. Major Nikolic stated that we could not go into the area because there were mines. And he stated that when you go in there it was not very, very wise to do so. So we were not allowed to go with impartial observers to check the line and see if we were talking about the same line. So it's very difficult to say if Serbs went into the demilitarised zone or Muslims went out because we are talking about different lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And those lines that were manned by Serbs, were they included into the demilitarised zone? Could you please provide direct answers and short answers. And only if the Trial Chamber allows you, you can go on talking. Otherwise, we are going to waste time without completing our task. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you ask a question, you should allow the witness to answer in the way which is a proper way to deal with the problems you raise with your questions. There may be some instances that a witness is not answering just -- and focusing and the core of your question, but this was not necessary to remind the witness at this stage. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, please could you listen to this and answer my questions that I will have after I have read the text. This is what Naser Oric is saying, and I'm quoting from the penultimate paragraph, the one above the last one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the text please be scrolled down a little so I can read from it. And it is the previous page in English. Thank you. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is the text entitled, "Guards Along the Lines." And I quote: "We didn't want Chetniks to see the weapons that we had not handed in. That would have been an argument for them to refuse signing the agreement, or to do who knows what. We had some 2.000 barrels; I knew that for a fact. And I didn't even know about all of the weapons. The weapons were being hidden. We kept some 20 cannons with four barrels. We made single barrel cannons of them so in the end we ended with a kind of anti-aircraft cannons. Let me explain. We hid every single barrel that we managed to capture from Chetniks, and when there was an action, we took them out. Everybody hid weapons from everybody else. Only the boldest ones, real soldiers, reported what they had. Others were keeping them in hiding until they were needed. It is all understandable. So we had probably approximately 4.000 barrels." And then he goes on to say that that became manifest during the breakthrough towards Tuzla, without a brigade in Zepa. Please tell us, were you aware of Muslims hiding the quantity, such a large quantity of weapons, as described by Naser Oric in this interview?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated yesterday, we were aware that there were weapons hidden by the Muslims inside the enclave. We were not aware of the amount of weapons that were hidden, nor the sort of weapons that were hidden. The only thing we could do is whenever we saw armed men or weapons in houses where we were able to go into, to confiscate them and store them in the weapon collection sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And when Muslims left the area, did it turn out that they indeed had about 4.000 barrels as Naser Oric states in this interview? Did that turn out to be true during the breakthrough towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps the General or the witness can give us an idea of barrels. I know barrels of oil and barrels of wine, but barrels of weapons, I'm not sure anyone here knows precisely what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Perhaps the witness should answer the question first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think when we are speaking about barrels, we are speaking about long-rifled guns, long weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was if it turned out "that they indeed had about 4.000 barrels," whatever that is, "as Naser Oric states in his interview." Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But when we are talking about 4.000 barrels, in my imagination we are talking about 4.000 weapons, so that can be pistols, that can be long rifles, but also rocket launchers, small rocket launchers, or small hand-grenade launchers. That's, in my opinion, the translation of the barrels he is stating over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As you indicated earlier, you have no information about the amount of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we have no information about the amount of weapons. And maybe I can directly answer the question of Mr. Tolimir. When a lot of men between 17 and 60 left the enclave on the 10th of July, I saw a lot of men gathered in the town of Srebrenica, lots of them were armed, but of course it was -- it was dark, and lots of them were already moving in the north-western direction. We didn't know where they would go. But at that moment we saw that there were armed men walking in the north-western direction. And also at that moment we did not know the amount of weapons they carried with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: People whom you saw, did they participate in the breakthrough that is referred to by Naser Oric in his interview, or did they go in some other direction?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people I refer to went in a big column in the north-western direction out of the town of Srebrenica, and I don't know where they went. And, later, I heard that there was a try to break through in the direction of Tuzla, but at that moment I did not know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During your patrols before the fall of Srebrenica, did you see armed Muslims walking around, and how often did you see them?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have seen armed Muslims walking around. I don't know the frequency of it, but we saw them frequently. All the time we saw armed Muslims. As I told you, we tried to disarm them and store the weapons in the weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell how successful your attempts were? Could you translate your success into a certain quality -- quantity of weapons that were taken from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you a quantity because we did our utmost to get the weapons without going so far that it was the ultimate goal to get the weapon and even try to shoot people to get the weapons. We just tried to catch them and disarm them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce the second column of this interview, the third paragraph, under the title: "The Demilitarisation of Srebrenica." Can you see where it says "the demilitarisation of Srebrenica," can you please move the document to the right -- or, rather, to the left. Thank you. And it is page 2 in English. Now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where it says "the demilitarisation of Srebrenica," I'm reading the first paragraph -- or, rather, the second paragraph: "So we handed over to the UNPROFOR only some of the weapons, for instance, two tanks. We had had five tanks, but since we didn't have any fuel for them, we had to burn some down." Could you please look at the advice provided to him by Naser Oric when it came to surrendering weapons. Could you please look at the penultimate line in the interview just below the image depicted in the text, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And below the photo, could you please show the second paragraph, the sixth line through the tenth line in that paragraph. Thank you. Go a bit further to the right, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm not aware that the witness is able to read Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So that you should give an indication where in the English translation he will find this passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the third page in English. And here we see the penultimate paragraph, line 6 in that paragraph, the second from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic also participated in this interview, and he says: "I ordered that those things that were not in a good working order be surrendered."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now continue with the column on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to know the exact part in English. I don't find it. The witness will not find it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. It's the fifth paragraph on the English side where it says, "Sefer Halilovic intervenes." That's in the first line of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I read the part where it says: "I ordered you to hand over the weapons that were out of order, and that's what you did. And we're talking about 200 barrels all together, including those home-made and useless rifles, plus some heavy weaponry, which you couldn't hide." My question is this: Firstly, does it transpire from this that Naser Oric, when he mentions 200 barrels, uses that word to describe long-rifled guns? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't look in the mind of Naser Oric, but when we are speaking about the barrels as stated before, I think we are talking about weapons, long and short weapons, pistols, and all those kind of things. And when we are talking about the 200 rifles now in this context, I think those were also the small arms, so the pistols and the hand-made guns that were stored in the weapon collection point. They were not only the hand-made weapons in the weapon collection point but also a lot of very good and useful weapons which were taken from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it transpire from the interview which also involved Sefer Halilovic who was commander during the demilitarisation that the commander of the BiH army ordered Naser Oric not to hand over all the weapons to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I read over there. But when we are talking about the period that this happened, I think it started in the period when General Morillon declared it as a safe haven in Srebrenica, a Canadian company came in, and they started to disarm the Muslims. And I think after that, from January 1994, the first Dutch Battalion came in and went on with the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what you have just told us, can you tell us whether it was General Morillon who declared Srebrenica a safe haven or whether it was owing to the Security Council and the agreement signed by the parties to that effect?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, I think I have to -- mind my words a little bit. As we all know, General Morillon was standing on the PTT building in the town of Srebrenica and declared that he would take care of the population and made a statement as if it was a safe haven. I think that's what I remember now. And, of course, we come to the same point as we stated before: it's not for a commander on the ground to declare an area as a safe haven; it is a UN topic, and it has to be done by the UN, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're not going to go into the origins of the agreement on demilitarisation and who signed it and how the area fled. We have already had testimony about that. We will move now to a different topic that I announced yesterday, mainly what I asked you yesterday: Was the attack on the enclave announced to you beforehand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before we move on to that topic, I would like to tender this document. 1D329. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll now go back to a passage that I quoted to you yesterday from your statement, page 3, paragraph 5, where Colonel Vukovic told you, if you remember, that due to constant incidents at Observation Post Echo, the Serbian forces were forced to intervene. So it was announced to you. Let me ask you, did the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo ever send a protest note picking up on the information they got from Serbs about the attacks emanating from the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I cannot answer that question because I was not in the direct line of command of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, so I think this is a question for commander of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then answer a question that you do know an answer to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can see 1D350.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is a statement you gave in Zagreb on the 22nd July, 1995, just after the end of your mission in Srebrenica, and you said something I'm interested in on page 2 in Serbian. I'm quoting what you said, and now we have it in English. Now both are in English. In fact, it's Dutch and English. You say: "The conduct of the BH army at OP-F was the straw that broke the camel's back. As the Bosnian Serb army," you call it Bosnian Serb army instead of VRS, "as the Bosnian Serb army continued to advance, the BH kept taking positions behind the observation posts, but the personnel of the observation posts were snappy after the fall of OP-E and the death of van Renssen and kept calling Section 5 forward. Rave and Captain Melgers had spent two days holding discussions with Ramiz, and that's Ramiz Becirovic, the Muslim commander in Srebrenica. They kept holding discussions with Ramiz to enforce freedom of movement for vehicles. But Ramiz did not have central leadership of the troops and did not have any information on the attacks. And Section 5 could not take over leadership of the BH." Have you read this passage in your language? Can you tell me what does the acronym CE 5 mean?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Section 5 was -- were the liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say this communication section could not take over leadership of the BH army. Was the situation so critical that somebody needed to take over command of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the communication section, it was the liaison section. The situation was that Ramiz was not able to order all his troops to guarantee our freedom of movement, so, of course, we had a feeling that nobody was really in charge, because when the highest commander on the scene is not able to order his troops what to do, then you've got a problem. And, of course, we were also not able to take over from Ramiz and command the BiH army over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after reading this, can you recall whether van Renssen died at Observation Post E, how he died, and who killed him?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we answered the question yesterday. I don't know exactly. I think it was OP Foxtrot he came from, when the manning of the OP returned via dirt road. Muslim civilians tried to stop him on the end of the road, they tried to stop the APC. The APC did not stop, carried on, and at that moment either a hand-grenade was thrown or a gun was shot that caused the death, at the end of the day, of the soldier van Renssen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this passage I read, you referred to Ramiz Becirovic. Is that the Ramiz Becirovic who in practice and officially stood in for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly what were these discussions with Ramiz about?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What discussions are you referring to? Because all the time during the six months we dealt with Ramiz. So could you be a little bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I meant the discussions referred to in this passage I quoted where you say that there was a straw that broke the camel's back and you talked to Ramiz for two days to get freedom of movement for vehicles. If you have anything to add to that, that would be nice. If not, I'll take it that you have given your answer already.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it is the same answer as I gave you yesterday. When the OPs in the southern part were attacked, at that moment we also had no freedom of movement to play the game of going back and going forward in the way we used to do. That was the problem for us, that our hands were tied to do our job in a normal military way because the Muslims stood behind us and had only one thing, that was, UNPROFOR should go forward and attack the enemy. That does not fit in our military way of acting, and that was the reason, for example, why the southern OPs went forward and surrendered to the Serbs. And, of course, that was -- this was going on also in the western part - correction, in the eastern part - and we had no freedom of movement and could not do our job in the way that we wanted to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at the last paragraph on the right page which begins with the words "note," and it says, "Rave". NB, nota bene, Rave. Rave says what is described in the next passage happened on the 11th of July, but the incident took place on 10 July. PG, according to Rave, the BH army had taken an M-4S tank, or an M-48 tank, and were using it to fire on Position B4. As a result, Hageman moved forward to the south and took fire from the BH army tank. According to Rave, it later became clear that this was a Bosnian Serb army tank. S5 then went to Ramiz to calm the spirits among the ranks of the BH army. Ramiz then went forward and came back with a message that the BH Army did not have a tank there, and that the BH army in place had been ordered to grant the UNPROFOR freedom of movement. While pulling out one of the APCs of the UNPROFOR, Hageman again took fire from - and there is something illegible, we don't know whom he took fire from. So this is the end of the quote. When exactly did the BH army seise that one tank that I -- that is referred to in this passage?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't even remember that I ever stated that the BiH had an M-48 tank. And when I read this passage now, I think they also didn't. I think there was a misunderstanding that maybe somebody thought that the BiH had an M-48 tank, and the only thing I know from I think it was Captain Hageman during that time, he was the one on the 11th of July, early in the morning, went forward with his APC to see if the Serb attack still was going on because that was one of the things we needed to be aware of for asking support from our higher echelons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you speak of support, can you tell us if you know when you were able to ask for support from the higher echelons of your force?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my knowledge, on the 10th of July we had a meeting, commander DutchBat had a meeting and I attended also the meeting, with the Muslim and the civilian leaders in the enclave, where command of DutchBat informed them that there would be air support. When the VRS attack continued the next morning by daylight, to be sure that the VRS was continuing their attack, we had to send forward an APC to check if it really was true. And when the APC was shot at by the VRS, it was confirmation. And I think that was also the time that commander of the Dutch Battalion asked for air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have to go into reconnaissance to see if it was an attack on the -- of the Bosnian Serb army or could you see it with the naked eye? If they were attacking you, you must have seen they were attacking.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the night, the attacks stopped. And in the morning, early in the morning, an APC went forward to see what would happen and to see how far they could go forward. At least, that's the impression I've got now. And at that moment when he was going forward, he was attacked by VRS fire. So that was first confirmation that the attack was still going on. And from that moment on, I remember that the attacks started again and the VRS moved farther upward north.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they, that APC, provoke the attack? Did it go into the VRS territory without prior notification? Did it get out of bounds of the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The APC was in the town of Srebrenica that night. It went to the southern border of the town of Srebrenica, so it was inside the enclave several kilometres. So the VRS was already several kilometres inside the enclave. So normally we should have had freedom of movement over there, because we were clearly visible as UN troops because we were in white APCs with big UN letters on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on the 10th and the 11th, these white APCs with the UN logo, did they fire on the firing positions of the Army of Republika Srpska as they were ordered?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on the spot and I think I can be for sure that they got the order to fire overhead and not to fire on the positions of the Bosnian Serb army -- the VRS army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll look at that later. Can you now explain to the Trial Chamber where is this B4 position from which the Muslim side fired at you using seised M-48 tank, the incident after which you discussed something with Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is a misstatement of the record, and it's contrary to the document he read from and contrary to the witness's answer on that point. That's inappropriate thing to do. That throws chaos and falsity into the record and should not be done. That has been cleared up. Clearly, I've not objected to this time, but that kind of injection of material is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you referring to this debriefing note we had on the screen when you have formulated your question? And if so, can you tell us which part of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to this nota bene from the text. In the Dutch version, it's the second sentence. And at the end of the sentence, we see Position B4. I asked the witness to explain where this B4 position is in relation to what I've just read. In English, it's the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the previous page. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no problem with the witness explaining B4. The problem is General Tolimir's question assumed and contained the -- that there was a BiH tank. And there was no such BiH tank. The BiH did not have a tank. That's clear in the thing he referred to, somebody at first thought they might have had one and then by the end of the paragraph it's clear that was mistaken; it was a Serb tank. The witness cleared that up and said there was no tank. And now he's gone back and said, Where is the -- or, Talk to us about the tank that the BiH had. I mean, that's just absurd. It's game playing. It's the same games he was playing with UNPROFOR at the time and it's not appropriate for the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, can you -- Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe it is completely inappropriate for Mr. McCloskey to say that it's the same game that Mr. Tolimir had played with the UNPROFOR back in 1995. It's very, very inappropriate, especially in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, can you explain the sentence: According to Rave, the BiH had taken an M-4S tank and were using it to fire on position B4? Can you explain this sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do it in the same way as I did before. I think there was a rumour that the BiH had an M-48 tank from the VRS and that they were shooting at the position B4. The question was, Position B4, I really don't know where it is because that's the operational situation from the Bravo Company at that moment. Later on, it seemed that it was not an M-48 tank that was in hands of the BiH, but it was a VRS tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's, again, a translation problem. In the English text it is M-4S, but in the Dutch version it is M-48.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's an M-48 tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I ask you, have you seen this document called "Debriefing Sergeant Major 1B Rave" before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Has this debriefing taken place on the 22nd of July, 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had an operational debriefing in Zagreb on that date. It was just an odd debrief. Never saw the results of those -- of this debriefing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was the person who interviewed you that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day, I was interviewed by the Colonel Lemon [phoen], the second in command of the 11th Air Mobile Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know a person of the name Professor Dr. P.H. Groen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've heard the name before. And as you can see, at the end of the text, he is the investigation leader from the section military history from the Dutch army, and I don't know if he was on the spot at that moment. I only know that I was debriefed by the Colonel Lemon at that moment. And all the, let's say, key players, I think 20 or 25 persons who had possibly useful information were debriefed at that moment in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You didn't sign this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that's what's also stated in the end of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tolimir, have you finished your examination on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do not intend to ask anything further about this document because the Prosecutor seems to mind. I was not quoting my words, I was quoting from the witness's statement given in Zagreb. But I have nothing further on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, just a moment. As for notification of potential evidence and exhibits we wanted to use, by mistake unfortunately it was not sent to Ms. Stewart but it was sent to Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Vanderpuye, Mr. Elderkin, and other members of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mean the list of exhibits to be used with this witness? That may be checked by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've determined that is -- that is correct, and I'm sure it won't be a problem again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. There are some minutes left before the break. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since there are just a few minutes, I won't move to the next topic. I just want to ask you, Were you in Srebrenica on the 11th and 12th of July when the people gathered around the petrol station where Ramiz Becirovic was giving his speech? Sorry, it was the 10th and the 11th July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 10th of July, I was in Srebrenica. I don't know if Ramiz given a speech over there. I could look in my notes specifically where I was at that time. In the evening, I think around 11.00, I went with commander of the Dutch Battalion to the PTT building where the military and civilian leaders of the enclave were assembled, and we had a meeting over there and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that later. Were you at the gas station when a mortar fire was opened? We saw it in that video-clip, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what video-clip you are referring to. And on the gas station where mortar fire was opened, the only thing we talked about yesterday was possible mortar fire, at least a grenade was falling on the compound of the Bravo Company. So I don't know what gas station you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This part of the trial video was not used yesterday during the examination of Mr. Rave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind the Muslim mortar fire on the 10th, when people gathered in Srebrenica. We are going to show you the scene or a still from the film. My assistant is going to show you, and then I will continue putting questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we should do that after the break. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Will the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Gajic will now play this footage so we can ask our questions of the witness, because we seem to have put some questions to him that he was unable to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, please, having seen this scene, can you tell us if you were there, and do you remember that this mortar fired from this position at the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there, and I have not seen this mortar fired. I even don't know exactly where this spot is at this moment. So I was not there, and I have not seen anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is it from the Bravo base?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I just said, I really don't even recognise the spot exactly where this is because I haven't been in Srebrenica for the last 10 or 12 years I think. So I don't recall the spot at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Since you can't remember, I won't have any more questions for you. I have to tell you that this scene depicts the mortar fire from the position and it hadn't been provoked by the fire from the VRS. I just wanted to ask you whether the monitors registered this incident and whether they reported it or recorded it in their log-book regarding firing activities on the ground?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if monitors registered it because I don't have the possibility to look inside the registers of the UN monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce D20, page 38, paragraph 3.58.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a report based on a debriefing which says, amongst other things -- and I'm going to quote once we receive paragraph 3.58 and when we receive it in the English version for your benefit, sir. Thank you. We will see it in a minute, I suppose. Paragraph 3.58. Thank you. It's the last paragraph, and we can see it now. It says in the first sentence, and I'll read: "On Monday 10 July, the commander of OP-M received orders from the C-Company commander to co-ordinate with the BiH army. That same evening, fighting broke out among the BiH army soldiers, resulting in dead and wounded." And thereafter, towards the end, it says: "When the two BiH army soldiers with the anti-tank weapons attempted to prevent their departure, they were shot in the head by the BiH army leader." Could you tell the Trial Chamber anything about what happened there, about this fighting that broke out among the BiH army soldiers and the resulting casualties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know about this incident is approximately what is stated in this debriefing. I was not there on the spot, and I have no more information from my memories. I -- for sure nothing in my notebooks about this incident, so I really can't give you any more information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you can't tell us anything, I won't have any more questions with this regard. And now could you please tell us whether, during the night between the 10th and 11 July, 1995, the DutchBat commander held a meeting with the military and civilian authorities in Srebrenica in the postal office building?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order for me to be able to put questions to you, I would like the Court to produce 1D351. This is an additional statement that this witness provided in Assen on the 3rd of October, 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You stated in Assen, and I quote: "During the night between the 10th and 11th July" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, which page are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please produce the second page. I didn't notice that what we see is the first page only. Can we see the first paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says here: "On the night of 11 July 1995, he attended a meeting at which the entire ABH military and civilian leadership and the civilian authorities in the enclave were present. During that meeting, Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans stated that unless the Bosnian Serb army withdrew from the enclave and stopped the attack on Srebrenica and the blocking positions, a massive air-strike would ensue. There was no mention of the number of aircraft, but, rather, of the fact that all targets in the immediate surroundings of the enclave would be put out of action. Colonel Karremans even spoke of sections of an area of one square kilometre which would disappear from the map." And based on what I've just quoted, could you tell us what you remember from that meeting? What did Karremans say about NATO air-strikes at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all I remember is stated in this debriefing. He was speaking about a massive air-strike, so not close-air support but a massive air-strike. And I think at that moment he explained to the leaders in the enclave what he meant was a massive air-strike, there would be a fixed-wing aircraft with a lot of arms, even cannons, in it, and they would be able to wipe out a square kilometre in a part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How could Mr. Karremans promise such an intense air support and air-strikes on the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska? What did he base that on?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see in the same point, I state over there that I really don't know where the information is coming from, but I suspect that the source is either not his command or BH command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether that meant any changes to the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica if NATO used massive air-strikes on the Republika Srpska targets?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think I'm not the right person to ask that question. I think that's a question that should be asked in the chain of command a little bit higher up. I even think somewhere in Sarajevo or maybe even in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted, please, in view of the fact that the witness speaks about the same things in the following parts of his debriefing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is here testifying. He certainly can be and should be questioned about his prior statements, but putting in the complete statement of a witness each time he testifies is really -- I don't know the reason for that. He's here to be questioned, and it's a precedent that would potentially swamp you with an untold number of statements. So unless there's a particular reason, it would not be, in this system, I think, appropriate. Unless there's a reason the Court wants to see it. And we can also arrange, as I think I've done before, to provide Courts with all statements of all witnesses, which it may be more appropriate in other systems, though that would incredibly swamp you, given how long this case has gone. So unless there's a particular reason for this, I would -- I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, do you remember this statement? Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this statement before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I signed this one, yes. But I signed it -- I think this is the debriefing. I don't know, is this from the summary or my own debriefing? Because we gave our first debriefings in Assen during that time, and I think this is from the debriefing in Assen, and I think this is only a part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we perhaps see the last page of it. If I'm not mistaken, this is the third page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the last page, I think, because this statement was made after a telephone call and not signed, on the 2nd of October, I think. But in my opinion it belongs to two or three parts of the debriefing Srebrenica we gave. In the first part of the debriefing, we had interviewers who were not exactly aware about all the abbreviations and the whole situation in the enclave, so -- and in that debriefing I also told at the end that the big lines were correct but in detail there could be a lot of mistakes because of the interviewers did not exactly know what happened during that time, did not know exactly the acronyms and all those kind of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You see on the left side of the screen handwriting, a signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have heard the objection by Mr. McCloskey. Can you give us further information about the purpose of tendering this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness attended the meeting during which the UNPROFOR mandate was changed, as well as the agreement which was unilaterally changed by the UNPROFOR commander. I would like that to be admitted. The witness said that he signed the statement, he said that he stated that, and that's why I'm tendering this into evidence. Besides, you can see that one side was being stopped by an attempt to destroy everything within a one-kilometre zone. Did UNPROFOR have the right to do that? Did they have the right to interfere and by assisting one side, destroy the other side? Was that the UNPROFOR mandate indeed? The witness did not want to respond; rather, he suggested that I should ask others about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, did you attend that meeting of the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we are speaking about the meeting on the 10th of 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 10th, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in which Colonel Karremans announced the possible air-strikes. I also told that I'm willing to answer the question but I'm not able to answer a question about decisions taken on the level of the UN -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know if you personally attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of course, we can discuss at length if we need every document. But on the other hand, this is a document signed by this witness related to this case. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 853 in the Krstic case transcript, and that's the same page where the same meeting is discussed, it says, and I quote: "At that moment, outside of the postal office building, there were a lot of armed men who carried rifles, machine-guns, rocket-launchers, and hand-held rocket-launchers. When we entered the postal office building, the military and civilian authority members were all there. They were all wearing uniforms. And there were a lot of them who also carried arms." My question to the witness based on what I have just read is this: Did you ask anybody among them where all those weapons had come from? How come they had so many weapons on them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't ask that question. And I also don't know -- well, I can imagine why we didn't ask that question, because there were a lot of other important things that happened at that moment. The enclave was attacked. So I think that's why we not even thought about it, at least I didn't think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you send a report to your superior command in Sarajevo or in Zagreb about what you had seen in the postal office building and also about what had been said at the meeting in the postal office building?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not send a report because that was not up to me to do, but I can imagine that Colonel Karremans, as battalion commander, sent a message up in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they informed that you had promised or threatened that you would destroy everything within a one-kilometre zone around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "were they informed," I think you mean the higher echelons. As I stated before, I don't know what was in the report of Colonel Karremans to the higher echelons, so I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 857, lines 11 through 23, you explained some of the events which took place on the 11th of July, and I quote: "At that moment, we did not have any other option but to try and take people to Potocari because Potocari was probably the only safe place for us. We realised that the VRS army had taken over Srebrenica, and that's why we asked them to start moving to Potocari. But there was a problem there; they didn't want to leave the base because that was the place where they felt safe. And then at 2.00 air-strikes began. There were several aircrafts involved. And I believe that after that the local population started trusting us a bit more because something had happened and they tried to move in the direction of Srebrenica." Based on what I have just read, my question is this: Whose idea was it for you to take the population from the base where they were at the moment to the base in Potocari? Just give us a name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we receive an answer, I would like to know the page number of the Krstic transcript because it was not -- is not in our today's transcript. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that's page 857, lines 11 through 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we check to see if -- that "moving in the direction of Srebrenica" is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see the document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think, in the context, that might have been Potocari. But, again, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is P1004, page 857. We should have that on the screen. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe to save time, just as Mr. Tolimir said, and I quote from the transcript page: "They did try to move in the direction of Potocari." That's what Mr. Tolimir said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need page 857. Yes. Thank you. Can you see that passage on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it. Mr. Tolimir asked me the question to give him a name who decided to send the people up to Potocari. Well, I can't give him a name. I think it was something that grew during that time. The compound of Bravo Company was overcrowded, a lot of refugees were around the compound. We were not able to bring the wounded who came from the hospital to the trucks on the compound of the Bravo Company to put the wounded in the trucks and then bring them to Srebrenica, so we had to do -- to Potocari. We had to do something. And I think it grew and we all together decided - and all together I mean the commander of the Bravo Company; Major Boering, who was there; and myself - that the best way was to get refugees towards Potocari because there was much more space than on the small compound in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you can't give us any names. But could you tell us whether that was at the initiative of UNPROFOR representatives from the Bravo Company that you just mentioned? Just tell us that for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it was an initiative of the UNPROFOR to get the people to the best place where they could stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Had you already prepared that Potocari base for the accommodation of the civilian population that would be sent from the Bravo Company base to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing was prepared. The only thing I know is -- was that the base in Potocari was much bigger than the base in Srebrenica. And I also don't think that we communicated with the base in Potocari, because a lot of refugees were already going in the direction of Potocari. And the only thing we tried to do is to get the people from the compound, because they broke through the fences, also in that direction. On the compound in Srebrenica, we had no possibility to do anything else than dealing with refugees. So our normal military jobs, for example, going in or out with APCs, was not possible at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was it who transported people from the Bravo base in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the refugees went up to Potocari themselves, walking, because we had no possibility to bring them. We had some trucks at the Bravo Company. Most of the trucks were used to put wounded in, the wounded from the hospital, to bring them up to Potocari. The other trucks that were there were practically taken over by the refugees. They climbed into it, could open the roofs, and then the drivers drove up to Potocari. At the end of -- no, in the middle of the afternoon, I think, 3.00 or 4.00, myself and Mr. Boering took a jeep because we couldn't do anything more on the spot of the Bravo Company at that moment, we took a jeep with a lot of refugees in it and also drove to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did you use that jeep to transport refugees?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used that jeep to take some elderly people who couldn't walk themselves, to bring them to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now play the video. And let's see how refugees were being accommodated in the Potocari base. After that, I'll have questions for you, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Aleksandar. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Whose trucks are these which brought the refugees, and who organised this?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were trucks who were at the spot of the Bravo Company and went from the Bravo Company with the refugees, as you see most women and children, towards Potocari. As you can see, those trucks went into the compound and into the factory where the headquarter of the battalion was stationed and also the Charlie Company. Only, I think, about 5.000 refugees were able to go to the compound; the rest stayed outside the compound in the several factories around the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the men were, because, as you mentioned, we can only see women and children here?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you might have read in some of my statements or testimonies, in the night from the 10th to the 11th, most of the men between 17 and 60 years old went in the north-western direction and left the town of Srebrenica. In the town stayed only women children, elderly men, or wounded. Also in these trucks and also in our jeep we drove to Potocari were those kind of people, so elderly people or very young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the UNPROFOR assumed the obligation to put up the women and children at their base in Potocari and to evacuate them, as requested by General Nikolai and Karremans that was conveyed to Mladic, while the men would go off with their weapons on foot from Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we are mixing up now some things. We have to do it, I think, in my opinion, in the right sequence. When the enclave fell in the night, men with weapons on foot went from Srebrenica in a north-western direction. We didn't know where they went to at that moment. Then on the 11th, the VRS moved forward towards Srebrenica. A lot of refugees were going northward. The best thing we could do to provide them as much safety and security as possible was put them in the vicinity of the compound or even on the compound in Potocari; although, I also got the information that the VRS, and I don't really know how -- who told this, that the refugees were not allowed to go onto the base in Potocari. So because of preventing that they would see that we let refugees on the base, they made a whole in the fence in the south-eastern part of the compound and the people, most of the refugees, went to the base, went through the fence in the south-eastern part where the VRS in the northern part not could see that they entered the compound. And when you are talking about evacuation as requested by General Nikolai, that is stated afterwards, because that's the first thing that was brought up by Colonel Karremans in the 8.00 meeting in the Hotel Fontana. So between the starting of the flow of refugees from Srebrenica to Potocari, that's part one. Then we got the invitation for a meeting or arranged the meeting that we -- was -- we discussed yesterday. And then we went to Hotel Fontana, where Karremans told - and that was also new for me - that he had had contact with the General Nikolai to arrange an evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since General Nikolai asked Colonel Karremans to organise an evacuation, was that before this scene that we are now looking at? And when exactly was this happening, this scene we are seeing on the monitor now?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specifically answer that question because I was in the -- with the refugees and Colonel Karremans had telephone calls with, I think, north-east command and BH command where General Nikolai was. So I think somewhere in the afternoon of the 11th General Nikolai and Colonel Karremans had contact and discussed this, but I wasn't there, so I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: To avoid mistakes on the record, just tell us, the refugees that you transported in your vehicle from Bravo Company, were they all coming on the 10th, or was it also on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only on the 11th. On the 10th, nothing happened. Of course, people were walking around, but in the morning from the 11th, people broke through the fence of the Bravo Company and after that, in the end of the morning and the beginning of the afternoon, we tried to get them off the compound in the direction of Potocari. And after this, so on the 11th, you get the images from overcrowded trucks bringing refugees into the compound in Srebrenica. The rest of the refugees are walking the road from Srebrenica to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you really mean Srebrenica. You are recorded having said: "... after this, so on the 11th, you get the images from overcrowded trucks bringing refugees in toward the compound in Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in my opinion, it's the 11th that the video we just saw, that the 11th in the afternoon, the trucks, the overcrowded trucks, come to the compound in Srebrenica. The left compound -- correction, it's the compound in Potocari. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the reason why I asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That is corrected now. Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. One question by Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, witness, you were there during the evacuation of these people, evacuation to Potocari. Now, I would like to know what you felt. Maybe you had the opportunity to talk to some of these people. What was their feeling at the time? Did they feel that they were leaving for good or that they would come back? Did they feel that they were leaving on their own volition or were they forced to leave? Were you able to talk to the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not able to talk to the people at that moment because we hardly had no interpreters on the spot at that moment. The attack was launched, and, of course, most of the people had experiences with attacks from the VRS towards them, so they had very bad experiences. And it was their free will to take what they could take and try to find a safe place to go. For them, UNPROFOR was the only place in their mind where it was safe to go, because they still had the idea that we were able to protect them. And I don't know if they had the idea that they were leaving for good. I think they just fled because an attack was launched. Mortar shells and grenades landed into the town of Srebrenica and for them that was enough reason to try to flee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A moment ago you said in one of your answers that Muslims from the Bravo Company did not want to go to Potocari when you were trying to persuade them, and you finally gained their confidence after the NATO air-strikes and that is when they went to the Potocari base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. A part of the refugees, of course, went in the northern direction depending where they lived. But when they were on the compound of the Bravo Company, they didn't want to leave because they felt safe over there. We tried to convince them that we had to do our job there and this was not the best place to be, but they didn't want to leave.
